newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus leaders meet on humanitarian issues.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus leaders meet on humanitarian issues.

text.p: Cypriot leaders Glafcos Clerides and Rauf Denktash met on Thursday for discussions on humanitarian issues connected with the protracted Cyprus dispute.
The meeting, at the residence of UN envoy to Cyprus Gustave Feissel, started at 6.00 p.m. (1500 GMT). It is their second meeting in a week.

The talks between Clerides, President of Cyprus and leader of the Greek Cypriot community, and Denktash, leader of the Turkish Cypriot community, were expected to focus on the issue of missing persons, and Cyprus's entry talks to the European Union, due to start next year.

Sources said Clerides was expecting replies from Denktash to proposals submitted at their previous meeting, on Monday, regarding the procedures that could be adopted for the opening of mass graves on both sides.

The Greek Cypriots say the fate of 1,619 persons has been unaccounted for since the Turkish invasion of Cyprus's north in 1974. The Turkish Cypriot community say 803 Turkish Cypriots went missing during intercommunal fighting in the 60s and early 70s.
Denktash, whose breakaway state in northern Cyprus is recognised only by Ankara, is asking that Clerides suspend Cyprus's bid to become a member of the European Union.

The Turkish Cypriot community hotly opposes Cyprus's application to become a full European Union member, citing international treaties which bar the island becoming a member of an institution that guarantor power Turkey is not.
The informal talks in Nicosia are held in between U.N. sponsored talks designed to restart stalled negotiations for a settlement to the Cyprus problem.
The first round of talks were held in upstate New York in early July, while the second round is tentatively scheduled to take place in Switzerland.
Turkish troops seized northern Cyprus in 1974, invading in reaction to a Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece. Some 30,000 troops are stationed there.
The Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence.
